subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 17 periods = 680 minutes
Total: 17 periods · 11h 20min

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (lace around tablecloth), section 6.1 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Akshi wants to put lace all around a rectangular tablecloth 3 m long and 2 m wide; find the length of lace required using P = 2 × (l + b) = 10 m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Usha runs three rounds), section 6.1 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the total distance Usha travels if she takes three rounds of a square park of side 75 m; perimeter = 300 m, total distance = 900 m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find missing length of a rectangle whose perimeter is 14 cm and breadth is 2 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1b, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the side length of a square whose perimeter is 20 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1c, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find missing breadth of a rectangle whose perimeter is 12 m and length is 3 m.

time_bands.activity: Ask students to trace the outer edge of their textbook with a finger and count the sides. Establish that perimeter means the total distance around a closed shape, and invite students to state what they would need to measure for different shapes — a rectangle, a square, a triangle.

Work through Example (lace around tablecloth), section 6.1 p.131 ("Akshi wants to put lace all around a rectangular tablecloth....") showing that because opposite sides are equal, the four-side sum collapses to 2 × (l + b). Follow with Example (Usha runs three rounds), section 6.1 p.131 ("Find the total distance Usha travels if she takes three rounds....") to derive the square formula as 4 × side and extend it to multiple rounds.

Students solve Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.1 p.132 ("Find missing length of a rectangle whose perimeter is 14 cm...."), Figure it Out Q1b, section 6.1 p.132 ("Find the side length of a square whose perimeter is 20 cm...."), and Figure it Out Q1c, section 6.1 p.132 ("Find missing breadth of a rectangle whose perimeter is 12 m....") individually, applying both formulas in reverse to find missing dimensions.

Select two or three students to share their reasoning aloud. Draw attention to the structure of each solution — how the formula is rearranged — and consolidate the three formulas on the board: rectangle P = 2(l + b), square P = 4s, triangle P = a + b + c.

periods.teacher_notes: Build the formulas inductively: let students count sides and observe the pattern before stating the rule. A common error is applying P = 2(l + b) when only one dimension is known and forgetting to divide by 2 to recover the missing side — watch for this in Q1a and Q1c.

periods.activity_title: Fencing, Wiring and Running: Perimeter in Context

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: A wire bent into a 5 cm × 3 cm rectangle is straightened and re-bent into a square; find the side length of the square.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the third side of a triangle with perimeter 55 cm and two sides 20 cm and 14 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the cost of fencing a rectangular park 150 m × 120 m at ₹40 per metre.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: A rectangular field 230 m × 160 m is fenced with 3 rounds of rope; find the total rope length needed.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5a, section 6.1 p.132
homework.description: A 36 cm string is formed into a square; find the side length.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5b, section 6.1 p.132
homework.description: A 36 cm string is formed into an equilateral triangle; find the side length.

time_bands.activity: Present a quick oral puzzle: if a rectangle has perimeter 16 cm and one side is 5 cm, what is the other side? Students respond chorally, refreshing the formula structure before tackling applied problems.

Students work in pairs on Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.132 ("A wire bent into a 5 cm × 3 cm rectangle is straightened and re-bent into a square....") and Figure it Out Q3, section 6.1 p.132 ("Find the third side of a triangle with perimeter 55 cm...."). The key insight for Q2 — total wire length is conserved — is discussed after pairs share answers.

Class works through Figure it Out Q4, section 6.1 p.132 ("Find the cost of fencing a rectangular park 150 m × 120 m at ₹40 per metre....") and Figure it Out Q6, section 6.1 p.132 ("A rectangular field 230 m × 160 m is fenced with 3 rounds of rope...."). Emphasise that multi-round fencing multiplies the perimeter, not the sides.

Brief whole-class debrief: which step did students find trickiest? Introduce the homework items Figure it Out Q5a and Q5b, section 6.1 p.132 ("A 36 cm string is formed into a square / equilateral triangle...."), framing them as a continuation of the conservation-of-length idea.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often forget that multi-round fencing requires multiplying the full perimeter by the number of rounds — they sometimes multiply only one side. In Q2 the conservation of perimeter when reshaping is the key concept; pair discussion surfaces this well before whole-class consolidation.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.1 p.133
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the total distance Akshi covers in 5 rounds of the outer rectangular track (70 m × 40 m).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.133
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the total distance Toshi covers in 7 rounds of the inner rectangular track (60 m × 30 m); determine who ran further.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3a-f, section 6.1 p.133
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mark positions A, B, C on Akshi's track after 250 m, 500 m, 1000 m; mark X, Y, Z on Toshi's track after 250 m, 500 m, 1000 m.

time_bands.activity: Draw two concentric rectangles on the board — outer 70 m × 40 m and inner 60 m × 30 m — to represent Akshi's and Toshi's tracks. Ask students to compute each perimeter mentally before proceeding to the exercises.

Students solve Figure it Out Q1, section 6.1 p.133 ("Find the total distance Akshi covers in 5 rounds of the outer rectangular track....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.133 ("Find the total distance Toshi covers in 7 rounds of the inner rectangular track; determine who ran further...."). Pairs compare their comparison reasoning before sharing with the class.

Work through Figure it Out Q3a-f, section 6.1 p.133 ("Mark positions A, B, C on Akshi's track after 250 m, 500 m, 1000 m; mark X, Y, Z on Toshi's track...."). Students draw the tracks on grid paper, mark the starting corner, and count cumulative distance around the rectangle, wrapping around corners as needed. Discuss how 1000 m relates to the number of complete rounds.

Whole-class check of position markings. Highlight the wrap-around strategy: divide total distance by perimeter to find complete laps plus a remainder, then locate the remainder distance along the track sides in order.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently place position markers by dividing total distance by the number of sides rather than by the perimeter — watch for this in Q3. The Matha Pachchi scenario gives rich context for cumulative perimeter reasoning; encourage students to annotate the track diagram with cumulative distances at each corner.

periods.activity_title: Measuring Irregular Boundaries and Diagonal Units

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Estimate and Verify, section 6.1 p.134
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cut irregular paper shapes from a rough sheet; estimate total boundary length by eye, then measure with a scale or measuring tape to verify the perimeter. Also discuss whether the perimeter of a dot-grid triangle is 9 straight units or more than 9 units (diagonal vs. straight length).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (straight and diagonal units), section 6.1 p.135
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write the perimeters of four dot-grid figures in terms of straight (s) and diagonal (d) units.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5c, section 6.1 p.132
homework.description: A 36 cm string is formed into a regular hexagon; find the side length.

time_bands.activity: Each student cuts an irregular shape from a rough sheet and estimates its perimeter by eye, recording their guess. Introduce the idea that estimation is a skill: the boundary is the total path around, regardless of shape regularity.

Students carry out Estimate and Verify, section 6.1 p.134 ("Cut irregular paper shapes from a rough sheet; estimate total boundary length by eye, then measure with a scale...."). They measure the actual perimeter using a measuring tape or by laying string along the edge. Compare estimates to measurements and discuss sources of error.

Introduce dot-grid figures. Pose the question from Estimate and Verify, section 6.1 p.134: is the perimeter of a dot-grid triangle 9 straight units or more? Students then complete Figure it Out (straight and diagonal units), section 6.1 p.135 ("Write the perimeters of four dot-grid figures in terms of straight (s) and diagonal (d) units...."), recognising that diagonal sides are longer than straight sides of the same grid step.

Class discussion: why does expressing perimeter in mixed s and d units matter? Consolidate the convention that one diagonal unit equals √2 straight units, and assign Figure it Out Q5c, section 6.1 p.132 ("A 36 cm string is formed into a regular hexagon; find the side length....") as take-home practice linking regular-polygon perimeter to division.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly count dot-to-dot steps as equal regardless of direction — the comparison of straight and diagonal units corrects this. Circulate during the measurement activity to ensure students are laying string along the full boundary, not just the longest edge.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin, section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cut a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangular paper chit into two equal halves and rejoin in four different configurations (a–d); find the perimeter of each arrangement and then find an arrangement with perimeter 22 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin Q b, section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the perimeter of arrangement b (two 6 cm × 2 cm pieces joined in an L-shape with 2 cm overlap).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin Q c, section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the perimeter of arrangement c (two pieces joined in a T-shape).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin Q d, section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the perimeter of arrangement d (two pieces joined in a staircase configuration).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin (target 22 cm), section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Arrange the two 6 cm × 2 cm pieces to form a figure with perimeter exactly 22 cm.

time_bands.activity: Briefly establish the general regular-polygon perimeter rule: perimeter = number of sides × side length, noting that squares and equilateral triangles are special cases. Pose: if a regular pentagon has perimeter 30 cm, what is each side? Students answer mentally.

Students each cut a 6 cm × 4 cm paper rectangle into two 6 cm × 2 cm halves, as in Split and rejoin, section 6.1 p.136 ("Cut a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangular paper chit into two equal halves and rejoin in four different configurations...."). They explore arrangement a (rejoined as original), then begin recording the boundary for each new arrangement.

Students work through Split and rejoin Q b, section 6.1 p.136 ("Find the perimeter of arrangement b...."), Split and rejoin Q c, section 6.1 p.136 ("Find the perimeter of arrangement c...."), Split and rejoin Q d, section 6.1 p.136 ("Find the perimeter of arrangement d...."), and Split and rejoin (target 22 cm), section 6.1 p.136 ("Arrange the two 6 cm × 2 cm pieces to form a figure with perimeter exactly 22 cm....").

Class shares the perimeters found for each arrangement. Discuss why different configurations of the same pieces give different perimeters — linking this to how many side-lengths become internal (shared) when pieces are joined, thus disappearing from the boundary.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often count internal seams as part of the boundary — clarify that any edge where two pieces touch is no longer exposed. Encourage students to trace the outer boundary with a pencil to avoid this confusion when computing arrangements b, c, and d.

periods.activity_title: Nine Squares: Exploring Minimum and Maximum Perimeters

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Making it 'More' or 'Less', section 6.1 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Arrange or draw different connected figures made from 9 unit squares; find the smallest and largest possible perimeters, make a figure with perimeter 18 units, and explore the effect of attaching one more unit square to a figure of perimeter 24 units.

time_bands.activity: Each student draws a connected figure made from exactly 9 unit squares on grid paper and counts its perimeter. Compare three or four different students' figures by writing perimeters on the board — observe that same-area figures can have very different perimeters.

Students work through Making it 'More' or 'Less', section 6.1 p.145 ("Arrange or draw different connected figures made from 9 unit squares; find the smallest and largest possible perimeters...."), systematically testing compact arrangements (approaching the 3×3 square for minimum) and elongated arrangements (the 1×9 strip for maximum). They record each figure's perimeter in a table.

Students attempt the target from Making it 'More' or 'Less', section 6.1 p.145: make a connected figure with perimeter exactly 18 units, then explore what happens to the perimeter when a tenth unit square is attached to a figure that currently has perimeter 24 units, reasoning about which sides become shared.

Whole-class discussion: why is the compact 3×3 square the minimum? How many sides does each internal shared edge remove from the perimeter? Generalise: each additional shared edge reduces the perimeter by 2 units, so attaching compactly reduces the boundary more than attaching at a corner.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes try non-connected figures (pieces touching only at a corner); establish clearly that each square must share at least one full edge with another. Watch for the minimum perimeter — the 3×3 gives 12, not 10; students sometimes undercount by forgetting corners.

periods.activity_title: Area Formulas: Rectangles, Squares and Composite Subtraction

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (floor and carpet), section 6.2 p.137
textbook_items_in_class.description: A floor 5 m × 4 m has a square carpet of side 3 m laid on it; find the area of the floor that is not carpeted: 20 – 9 = 11 sq m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (four flower beds), section 6.2 p.137-138
textbook_items_in_class.description: A piece of land 12 m × 10 m has four square flower beds of side 4 m at the four corners; find the area of the remaining part: 120 – 64 = 56 sq m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: A rectangular garden 25 m long has area 300 sq m; find the width.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the cost of tiling a 500 m × 200 m plot at ₹8 per 100 sq m.

time_bands.activity: Ask students to draw a 4×3 rectangle on grid paper and count unit squares. Introduce area as the number of unit squares that fill the interior, then confirm the formula: area of rectangle = l × b, area of square = s². Extend to composite subtraction: whole minus the removed part.

Walk through Example (floor and carpet), section 6.2 p.137 ("A floor 5 m × 4 m has a square carpet of side 3 m; find the area not carpeted....") and Example (four flower beds), section 6.2 p.137-138 ("A piece of land 12 m × 10 m has four square flower beds of side 4 m...."). Draw diagrams for each, labelling dimensions before calculating.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.138 ("A rectangular garden 25 m long has area 300 sq m; find the width....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.138 ("Find the cost of tiling a 500 m × 200 m plot at ₹8 per 100 sq m...."). For Q2, guide students to notice the rate is per 100 sq m, not per 1 sq m.
Quick pair-check: students swap books and verify each other's solutions. Highlight the distinction between area (square units) and perimeter (linear units) — a common confusion — before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse which dimension to use when working backwards from area to find a missing side — insist on writing l × b = area before dividing. In the flower-bed problem, the subtraction of four separate beds must be completed before comparing to the whole; some students subtract only one bed and multiply separately.

periods.activity_title: Composite Areas: Splitting L-shapes and Frames

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: A coconut grove 100 m × 50 m; each tree needs 25 sq m; find the maximum number of trees.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4a, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: Split figure a (L-shaped composite) into rectangles and find its area in metres.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4b, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: Split figure b (rectangular frame) into rectangles and find its area in metres.

time_bands.activity: Draw an L-shaped figure on the board (dimensions visible). Ask students how they would find its area if they only know the rectangle formula. Elicit the idea of splitting into two non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas — or completing the outer rectangle and subtracting.

Students solve Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.138 ("A coconut grove 100 m × 50 m; each tree needs 25 sq m; find the maximum number of trees....") as a straightforward area-division problem, then discuss the real-world constraint that trees must fit without overlap.

Students work on Figure it Out Q4a, section 6.2 p.138 ("Split figure a (L-shaped composite) into rectangles and find its area....") and Figure it Out Q4b, section 6.2 p.138 ("Split figure b (rectangular frame) into rectangles and find its area...."). Students annotate their diagrams showing the split lines before computing sub-areas.

Compare two splitting strategies for Q4a (add two rectangles vs. complete-and-subtract) on the board, verifying they give the same answer. Reinforce that both approaches are valid and students should choose whichever involves fewer steps for a given figure.

periods.teacher_notes: For the frame in Q4b, students often attempt to split into only two rectangles and leave overlapping corners; guide them to use four edge-strips or the outer-minus-inner strategy. Labelling all dimensions before computing prevents arithmetic errors with multi-piece splits.

periods.activity_title: Tangram Area Reasoning: Equal, Double, and Multiple Areas

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using tangram pieces, explore and identify which pieces have the same area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine how many times bigger Shape D is compared to Shape C; describe the relationship between Shapes C, D, and E.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine which tangram shape has more area: Shape D or Shape F; give reasons.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine which tangram shape has more area: Shape F or Shape G; give reasons.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare the area of Shape A to Shape G; determine whether A is twice or four times as big as G.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of the big square formed with all seven tangram pieces in terms of the area of Shape C.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 6.2 p.139
homework.description: Arrange the 7 tangram pieces into a rectangle and state its area in terms of Shape C; give reasons.

time_bands.activity: Distribute tangram cut-outs (or have students use the textbook's tangram page). Introduce Shape C as the reference unit. Students physically compare pieces by overlaying — can any two pieces together cover another exactly?

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.139 ("Explore and identify which pieces have the same area...."), Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.139 ("Determine how many times bigger Shape D is compared to Shape C...."), Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.139 ("Which has more area: Shape D or Shape F?...."), and Figure it Out Q4, section 6.2 p.139 ("Which has more area: Shape F or Shape G?...."), giving reasons for each answer.

Students complete Figure it Out Q5, section 6.2 p.139 ("Compare the area of Shape A to Shape G; determine whether A is twice or four times as big....") and Figure it Out Q6, section 6.2 p.139 ("Find the area of the big square formed with all seven tangram pieces in terms of Shape C...."). Students must reason from their earlier comparisons rather than measuring directly.

Class shares Q6 reasoning. Record the area of the full tangram square in C-units on the board, and introduce Figure it Out Q7, section 6.2 p.139 as take-home exploration: can the same seven pieces form a rectangle with the same total area?

periods.teacher_notes: Tangram comparisons build area intuition before students have formal fractional-area tools — the key move is superimposing pieces, not calculating. Students often confuse shape and area; Q3 and Q4 are productive because D and F differ in shape but may have equal or unequal areas, prompting genuine reasoning.
materials: Tangram cut-outs (one set per student or pair)

periods.activity_title: Grid Estimation and the Area–Perimeter Relationship for Rectangles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare the perimeters of the square and the rectangle formed from the 7 tangram pieces; explain whether they are the same or different.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let's Explore (24 sq units), section 6.2 p.141
textbook_items_in_class.description: On grid paper, make as many whole-number rectangles as possible with area 24 sq units; identify which has the greatest perimeter (a), the least perimeter (b), and explore the pattern for area 32 sq cm (c).

time_bands.activity: Revisit Figure it Out Q8, section 6.2 p.139 ("Compare the perimeters of the square and the rectangle formed from the 7 tangram pieces; explain whether they are the same or different....") as a warm-up. Students discuss in pairs and share: two shapes with equal area can have different perimeters.

Students work on Let's Explore (24 sq units), section 6.2 p.141 ("On grid paper, make as many whole-number rectangles as possible with area 24 sq units; identify which has the greatest perimeter, the least perimeter, and explore the pattern for area 32 sq cm...."). They draw all factor-pair rectangles (1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6) and record dimensions and perimeters in a table.

Students replicate the investigation for 32 sq cm (factor pairs: 1×32, 2×16, 4×8) and compare the patterns. Guide the class to articulate: for a fixed area, the rectangle closest to a square has the smallest perimeter; the most elongated has the largest.

Summarise the area–perimeter relationship on the board as a two-way statement: same area, different perimeters; and same perimeter, different areas (recalling the wire-bending problem). This duality is central to the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: The exploration works best when students list all factor pairs systematically; if students miss a pair (e.g., 4×6 from 24), their table will be incomplete and their conclusion about the minimum may be wrong. Prompt systematic listing by starting from 1 and increasing the first factor until the two factors cross over.

periods.activity_title: House Floor Plans: Recovering Missing Dimensions

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (Charan's house), section 6.2 p.146
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using Charan's house floor plan (30 ft × 35 ft overall), find the missing room dimensions and total house area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (Sharan's house), section 6.2 p.147
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using Sharan's house floor plan (42 ft wide), find missing room dimensions and total area; compare areas and perimeters of both houses.

time_bands.activity: Display a simple rectangular floor plan on the board with one room's dimension missing and the total width labelled. Ask: how would you find the missing dimension? Establish the constraint that aligned room dimensions sum to the overall house dimension.

Students work through Figure it Out (Charan's house), section 6.2 p.146 ("Using Charan's house floor plan 30 ft × 35 ft overall, find the missing room dimensions and total house area...."). Guide them to annotate the plan with known values and use row/column sums to recover unknowns before computing any area.

Students tackle Figure it Out (Sharan's house), section 6.2 p.147 ("Using Sharan's house floor plan 42 ft wide, find missing room dimensions and total area; compare areas and perimeters of both houses...."). After computing, students write a brief comparison stating which house is larger in area and whether the house with more area also has the greater perimeter.

Quick debrief: did the house with greater area also have the greater perimeter? Discuss how the shape (elongated vs. compact) affects perimeter independently of area, connecting back to the factor-pair investigation.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often jump to area computation before recovering missing dimensions — insist they label all sides of the plan before calculating any area. The comparison at the end of the Sharan problem reinforces that area and perimeter are independent properties, a conceptually important insight for this chapter.

periods.activity_title: Area Maze Puzzles: Multi-step Sub-rectangle Reasoning

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qa, section 6.2 p.148
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given sub-rectangle areas 13, 26, and 15 sq cm in a 2×2 grid arrangement, find the missing fourth area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qb, section 6.2 p.148
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given two sub-rectangles of 10 sq cm each with dimensions 2 cm and 3 cm visible, find the missing area of the third sub-rectangle (3 cm × 2 cm top right).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qc, section 6.2 p.148
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given a composite figure with total height 15 cm, sub-rectangles of 42 sq cm and 60 sq cm with some dimensions given, find the missing top sub-rectangle area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qd, section 6.2 p.148
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given two stacked sub-rectangles with areas 38 sq cm and 18 sq cm and dimensions 4 cm and 5 cm visible, find the missing width (top side length) of the larger rectangle.

time_bands.activity: Show a simple 2-sub-rectangle figure on the board: one sub-rectangle is 3 cm × 4 cm with area 12 sq cm, the other has width 5 cm and unknown height. Ask: if the two sub-rectangles share the same height, can we find the second area? Establish the chain-reasoning strategy.

Students work on Area Maze Puzzles Qa, section 6.2 p.148 ("Given sub-rectangle areas 13, 26, and 15 sq cm in a 2×2 grid arrangement, find the missing fourth area....") and Area Maze Puzzles Qb, section 6.2 p.148 ("Given two sub-rectangles of 10 sq cm each with dimensions 2 cm and 3 cm visible, find the missing area...."). The strategy is to recover a shared dimension from a known area-plus-side before computing the unknown.

Students tackle Area Maze Puzzles Qc, section 6.2 p.148 ("Given composite figure with total height 15 cm, sub-rectangles of 42 sq cm and 60 sq cm, find the missing top sub-rectangle area....") and Area Maze Puzzles Qd, section 6.2 p.148 ("Given two stacked sub-rectangles with areas 38 sq cm and 18 sq cm, find the missing width...."). These require multi-step chains of division followed by multiplication.

Class debrief: which puzzle required the most steps? Students write a two-line description of the chain of reasoning for Qd on the board. Consolidate: area ÷ known side = unknown side; then use that side to find the next area.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in Area Maze Puzzles is assuming all sub-rectangles share the same dimension when they do not; encourage students to annotate the figure with every side length they derive before computing the next area. Qd requires finding a missing width, which means dividing area by height — students may try multiplying instinctively.

periods.activity_title: Cutting the Rectangle: Why a Triangle is Half

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Cut rectangle activity, section 6.3 p.142
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw a rectangle, draw one diagonal, cut along the diagonal to produce two triangles; check whether the triangles overlap exactly and have the same area. Repeat with rectangles of different dimensions and with a square. Use grid paper to verify the triangle-rectangle area relationship for both right triangles and non-right triangles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.143
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the grid, find the area of blue triangle BAD in rectangle ABCD.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.3 p.143
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the grid, find the area of red triangle ABE by decomposing into triangles AEF and BEF over sub-rectangles AFED and BFEC.

time_bands.activity: Each student carries out Cut rectangle activity, section 6.3 p.142 ("Draw a rectangle, draw one diagonal, cut along the diagonal to produce two triangles; check whether the triangles overlap exactly...."). They flip one triangle onto the other and observe congruence. Ask: what does this tell us about the area of each triangle compared with the rectangle?

Students repeat the cutting with a rectangle of different dimensions and then with a square, recording each rectangle's area and the resulting triangle's area. After three trials, students articulate the pattern: triangle area = ½ × rectangle area = ½ × base × height.

Students use grid paper to work through Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.143 ("Find the area of blue triangle BAD in rectangle ABCD....") by counting squares and verifying it equals half the rectangle's area. Then they tackle Figure it Out Q2, section 6.3 p.143 ("Find the area of red triangle ABE by decomposing into triangles AEF and BEF...."), following the decomposition argument for a non-right triangle.

Class discussion: does the formula ½ × b × h hold for the triangle in Q2 even though the apex E is not directly above a base vertex? Students verify numerically that triangle AEF + triangle BEF = ½(AFED) + ½(BFEC) = ½(ABCD). State the general principle.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes believe the diagonal must be from a specific corner — clarify that any diagonal works and both resulting triangles are congruent. The key conceptual step in Q2 is the decomposition into two sub-rectangles; if students see only the whole rectangle they may not accept the formula for the slanted triangle ABE.

items.prompt: A rectangle has a perimeter of 18 cm and a breadth of 3 cm. What is its length?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 cm. Using P = 2(l + b): 18 = 2(l + 3), so 9 = l + 3, giving l = 6 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply P = 2(l + b) and solve for the unknown length by dividing the perimeter by 2 and subtracting the known breadth.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student subtracted only the breadth once from the perimeter (18 − 3 = 15) without halving first, confusing the formula structure.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student halved the perimeter to get 9 and then subtracted only 3 once but doubled incorrectly, likely computing 2 × 6 as 12 rather than reading off l.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student computed P/2 = 9 and reported that as the length without subtracting the breadth, confusing half-perimeter with length.

inclusivity.support: Let the student write out 2(l + b) = 18 step by step and check each substitution with the formula.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find two more rectangles with perimeter 18 cm and state whether there is a rectangle with perimeter 18 cm and equal length and breadth.

exercise.description: Find missing length of a rectangle whose perimeter is 14 cm and breadth is 2 cm.

items.prompt: A square tile of side 4 m is placed in the centre of a rectangular room that is 8 m long and 6 m wide. What is the area of the room floor not covered by the tile?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 32 sq m. Area of room = 8 × 6 = 48 sq m. Area of tile = 4 × 4 = 16 sq m. Uncovered area = 48 − 16 = 32 sq m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute each area separately using the rectangle and square formulas, then subtract the smaller from the larger.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student found the room's area (48 sq m) but forgot to subtract the tile's area, stopping at the first calculation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student found only the tile's area (16 sq m) and reported it as the answer, reversing which area is required.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student subtracted only one side of the tile (4) from one dimension of the room (8 − 4 = 4) and then multiplied incorrectly, applying the subtraction to linear measures rather than areas.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to draw the room and shade the tile, then count grid squares outside the shaded region.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if a second identical tile is placed in an opposite corner, what is the uncovered area now, and does it change if the tiles touch?

exercise.description: A floor 5 m × 4 m has a square carpet of side 3 m laid on it; find the area of the floor that is not carpeted: 20 – 9 = 11 sq m.

items.prompt: Riya says: 'Among all connected figures made from 9 unit squares, the one that looks most like a square has the smallest perimeter.' Is Riya correct? Explain your reasoning using the idea of shared edges.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Riya is correct. The 3×3 square arrangement gives the smallest perimeter of 12 units. Each time two unit squares share an edge, that shared edge is removed from the total boundary — reducing the perimeter by 2 units. The compact 3×3 square maximises the number of shared edges (each interior unit square shares more edges with its neighbours than in an elongated arrangement), so it minimises the exposed boundary. A 1×9 strip, by contrast, shares only 8 edges (between 9 consecutive squares) giving perimeter 20, while the 3×3 square shares 12 edges, giving perimeter = 4×9 − 2×12 = 36 − 24 = 12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reason that each shared edge reduces the perimeter by 2, so maximising shared edges (achieved by the compact square shape) minimises total perimeter.

inclusivity.support: Have the student draw a 1×3 strip and a 3×3 block of three squares, count shared edges in each, and compare perimeters before tackling nine squares.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what arrangement of 9 squares gives the second-smallest perimeter — is it unique, or can several arrangements share that value? Justify with shared-edge counts.

exercise.book_ref: Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q1, section 6.3 p.145
exercise.description: Using 9 connected unit squares, find the smallest possible perimeter.

items.prompt: A connected figure of 9 unit squares has perimeter 20 units. Priya claims this must be the longest possible perimeter for any such figure. Explain whether Priya is correct, and justify your answer by describing the arrangement that gives the largest perimeter and why no arrangement can exceed it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya is correct. The largest perimeter is 20 units, achieved by arranging all 9 squares in a single 1×9 row. In this arrangement, consecutive squares share exactly 8 edges (one between each adjacent pair), so the total perimeter = 4×9 − 2×8 = 36 − 16 = 20. Any other connected arrangement requires at least as many shared edges (since connectivity means at least 8 shared edges for 9 squares), but branching or stacking squares creates additional shared edges beyond 8, reducing the perimeter below 20. Therefore the 1×9 strip, which minimises shared edges among all connected arrangements, gives the maximum perimeter of 20.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the principle that each shared edge reduces perimeter by 2, so the arrangement with the fewest shared edges (the linear strip) maximises perimeter.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to build a 1×5 strip first, count its perimeter, then add a sixth square in a corner position and recount — discussing why the perimeter changes.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: is there a connected figure of 9 squares with perimeter 19 units? Explain why or why not, using the parity of the perimeter formula.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 7 cm. Perimeter of rectangle = 2 × (9 + 5) = 2 × 14 = 28 cm. Wire length = 28 cm. Side of square = 28 ÷ 4 = 7 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the rectangle's perimeter to get the wire length, then divide by 4 to find the square's side.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student sketch both shapes and write the total wire length as a known quantity before finding the new side.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the same wire is re-bent into an equilateral triangle, what is each side? What shape gives the greatest area for this wire length?

items.prompt: A dot-grid figure has 3 straight sides of length 1 unit each and 2 diagonal sides. Write its perimeter in terms of straight units (s) and diagonal units (d). State which is larger: a perimeter of 5s or a perimeter of 3s + 2d?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Perimeter = 3s + 2d. Since one diagonal unit equals √2 ≈ 1.41 straight units, 2d ≈ 2.83s, so 3s + 2d ≈ 5.83s. This is larger than 5s. Therefore the figure with the diagonal sides has the greater perimeter.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Express the perimeter as 3s + 2d and compare by recognising that each diagonal unit is longer than one straight unit.

inclusivity.support: Let the student use a ruler on dot paper to measure one diagonal unit against one straight unit and confirm which is longer before comparing the perimeters.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: how many straight units would give the same perimeter as 3s + 2d? Express your answer as a decimal.

items.prompt: Two identical rectangular pieces, each 8 cm long and 3 cm wide, are joined along their 3 cm edges to form a new shape. What is the perimeter of the new shape?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 26 cm. When the two 8 cm × 3 cm pieces are joined along a 3 cm edge, the resulting shape is a 16 cm × 3 cm rectangle (or a shape where the two short edges become internal). Perimeter = 2 × (16 + 3) = 2 × 19 = 38 cm. Alternate arrangement: join along the 8 cm edges to make an 8 cm × 6 cm rectangle. Perimeter = 2 × (8 + 6) = 28 cm. Joining along the 3 cm edge with full overlap gives perimeter 38 cm; joining along the 8 cm edge gives 28 cm. The question specifies joining along the 3 cm edges: perimeter = 38 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Determine the dimensions of the combined shape after the two shared edges disappear from the boundary, then apply P = 2(l + b).

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to draw both pieces side by side on grid paper, mark the shared edge, then trace and count the outer boundary.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: can the two pieces be joined to give a perimeter of 26 cm? If so, describe the arrangement; if not, explain why.

items.prompt: Using exactly 9 unit squares joined edge-to-edge, Meena forms a connected figure. She claims its perimeter is 16 units. Show that 16 is a possible perimeter by stating how many shared edges the figure must have, and draw (or describe) one arrangement that achieves it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each unit square has perimeter 4 units. For 9 squares: total if separate = 4 × 9 = 36 units. Each shared edge removes 2 units from the perimeter, so perimeter = 36 − 2 × (number of shared edges). For perimeter 16: 36 − 2 × n = 16, so n = 10 shared edges. One arrangement: a 3×3 square has 12 shared edges (perimeter 12). To get 10 shared edges, use an arrangement with one square removed from the interior — for example, a 3×4 rectangle minus two corner squares (or a T-shape or cross shape with exactly 10 internal shared edges). A straightforward example: a 3×3 block with one extra square attached outside gives n = 12 shared edges (perimeter 12), so that is too compact. A correct example is an L-shaped figure: a 2×5 strip (8 shared edges, perimeter 20) does not reach 10. A 3×3 square minus one square (8 squares, not 9) is invalid. Valid example: arrange 9 squares as a 2×4 strip with one extra square attached at one end on the side — this yields 10 shared edges and perimeter 16. Another valid example: a 3×3 arrangement but with one square detached and placed to share only one edge on the outside.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use perimeter = 36 − 2n to find the required number of shared edges (n = 10), then describe a connected arrangement of 9 squares realising exactly 10 shared edges.

inclusivity.support: Give the student the formula perimeter = 4×9 − 2×n and ask them to solve for n before drawing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: which values of n (shared edges) are achievable for 9 connected unit squares, and which are not? List three achievable perimeters and explain why perimeter 11 is impossible.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 60 plants. Area of field = 36 × 15 = 540 sq m. Number of plants = 540 ÷ 9 = 60.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the total area using l × b, then divide by the area each plant requires.

inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the field is extended to 40 m × 15 m, how many more plants can be grown? What is the minimum field length (keeping width 15 m) that allows exactly 100 plants?

items.prompt: Two shapes are formed from the same set of seven tangram pieces. Shape P is a square and Shape Q is a rectangle. Ananya says their areas must be equal but their perimeters might differ. Is Ananya correct? Explain your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Ananya is correct on both counts. Since both shapes use all seven tangram pieces with no gaps or overlaps, the total area covered is the same in both cases — equal to the sum of the areas of all seven pieces. However, the perimeters can differ because area and perimeter are independent: a square and a rectangle can have the same area but different perimeters (a square has the smallest perimeter for a given area among all rectangles). So the two shapes have equal area but generally different perimeters.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Argue that area is conserved when pieces are rearranged without gaps, but perimeter depends on the shape's outer boundary and can change.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to verify with a specific numerical example: if the tangram square has side 4 units, what is its perimeter? If the rectangle is 2 units × 8 units with the same area, what is its perimeter?

items.prompt: A large rectangle is divided into two smaller rectangles side by side. The left rectangle has area 20 sq cm, and the right rectangle has area 30 sq cm. Both rectangles share the same height. The width of the left rectangle is 4 cm. Find the total width of the large rectangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 9.5 cm. Height = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm. Width of right rectangle = 30 ÷ 5 = 6 cm. Total width = 4 + 6 = 10 cm. (Verification: 5 × 10 = 50 = 20 + 30. ✓)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recover the shared height from the known area and width of the left rectangle, then find the right rectangle's width, and add both widths.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to label the shared height h and write two equations: 4h = 20 and w·h = 30, then solve in order.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if instead the total width is kept at 10 cm but the two sub-rectangle areas are swapped (left = 30, right = 20), does the height change? Explain.

exercise.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qa, section 6.2 p.148
exercise.description: Given sub-rectangle areas 13, 26, and 15 sq cm in a 2×2 grid arrangement, find the missing fourth area.

items.prompt: On a grid, a composite figure consists of a 6-unit × 4-unit rectangle with a triangle attached to one of its 6-unit sides. The triangle has its base along the 6-unit side and its apex 3 units above the base. Find the total area of the composite figure.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 33 sq units. Area of rectangle = 6 × 4 = 24 sq units. Area of triangle = ½ × 6 × 3 = 9 sq units. Total area = 24 + 9 = 33 sq units.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute rectangle area as l × b and triangle area as ½ × base × height, then add the two sub-areas.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to first identify and shade the rectangle and the triangle separately on grid paper, then compute each area before adding.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the height of the triangle were doubled to 6 units, by how many square units would the total area increase? What if the rectangle's length were halved instead?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.3 p.144
exercise.description: Find the area of composite figure a on the grid by dividing into rectangles and triangles.

items.prompt: Find the dimensions of a rectangle whose area equals the combined area of a 4 m × 7 m rectangle and a 3 m × 6 m rectangle. Give one valid pair of dimensions for your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Combined area = 4 × 7 + 3 × 6 = 28 + 18 = 46 sq m. One valid rectangle: 2 m × 23 m (since 2 × 23 = 46). Another valid example: 46 m × 1 m. Any factor pair of 46 is acceptable.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the sum of the two given areas, then express 46 as a product of two whole numbers to give the rectangle's dimensions.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to compute each area separately, add them, and then list factor pairs of the result starting from 1.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: how many whole-number rectangles have area 46 sq m? Which of these has the smallest perimeter?

items.prompt: Priya draws a rectangular border inside a sheet of paper that is 20 cm long and 15 cm wide. The border is 2 cm from each of the longer sides (top and bottom) and 2.5 cm from each of the shorter sides (left and right). What is the perimeter of the border rectangle?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 45 cm. Border length = 20 − 2 × 2.5 = 20 − 5 = 15 cm. Border breadth = 15 − 2 × 2 = 15 − 4 = 11 cm. Perimeter = 2 × (15 + 11) = 2 × 26 = 52 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract twice the offset from each paper dimension to get the border's dimensions, then apply P = 2(l + b).

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to draw the sheet and label the gaps on each side before computing the inner rectangle's dimensions.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what is the area of the strip between the paper edge and the border rectangle? Express it as (paper area − border area).

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 6.3 p.149
exercise.description: Draw a rectangular border on a page that is 1 cm from top and bottom and 1.5 cm from left and right sides; find its perimeter.
